verses.28:23: One who reproves a person will find greater favor afterward than one who flatters with the tongue.
verses.28:24: One who robs his father and his mother and says, "There is no transgression," is a partner to a destructive man.
verses.28:25: One with a greedy appetite stirs up contention, but one who trusts in the LORD will thrive.
verses.28:26: One who trusts in his heart is a fool, while one who walks in wisdom will be rescued.
verses.28:27: One who gives to the poor has no lack, yet one who hides his eyes abounds in curses.
verses.28:28: When the wicked rise, people conceal themselves, yet when they perish, the righteous multiply.
verses.29:1: A man repeatedly reproved who stiffens his neck will be shattered in an instant, and there is no healing.
verses.29:2: When the righteous multiply, the people are glad, but when a wicked person rules, people groan.
verses.29:3: A man who loves wisdom gladdens his father, but one who associates with prostitutes destroys wealth.
verses.29:4: A king establishes a land by justice, but a man of exactions tears it down.
verses.29:5: A man who flatters his neighbor spreads out a net over his footsteps.
verses.29:6: In the transgression of an evil man is a snare, but a righteous person shouts for joy and is glad.
verses.29:7: A righteous person knows the case of the poor; a wicked person does not understand knowledge.
verses.29:8: Men of scoffing inflame a city, but the wise turn back anger.
verses.29:9: When a wise man contends in court with a foolish man, he rages and laughs, and there is no rest.
verses.29:10: Men of bloodshed hate a blameless person, but the upright care for his life.
verses.29:11: A fool lets out all his spirit, but a wise person stills it in reserve.
verses.29:12: If a ruler listens closely to a word of falsehood, all his attendants are wicked.
verses.29:13: A poor man and an oppressor meet together; the LORD brings light to the eyes of both of them.
verses.29:14: A king who judges the poor in truth—his throne will be established forever.
verses.29:15: A rod and reproof impart wisdom, but a boy left unrestrained puts his mother to shame.
verses.29:16: When the wicked multiply, transgression multiplies, but the righteous will see their downfall.
verses.29:17: Discipline your son, and he will grant you rest, and he will give delights to your soul.
verses.29:18: Without vision, a people goes unrestrained, but the one who observes the law is blessed.
verses.29:19: By words a servant will not be disciplined, for he understands, yet there is no response.
verses.29:20: Have you seen a man who rushes in his words? There is greater hope for a fool than for him.
verses.29:21: One who pampers his servant from youth will see him become an heir in the end.
verses.29:22: A man of anger provokes strife, and a person of wrath is full of transgression.
verses.29:23: A person's pride brings him low, but one who is lowly of spirit lays hold of honor.
verses.29:24: One who shares with a thief hates his own life; he hears the curse, yet does not report it.
verses.29:25: Dread of people sets a snare, but the one who trusts in the LORD will be lifted to safety.
verses.29:26: Many seek a ruler's face, yet from the LORD comes a person's justice.
verses.29:27: An abomination to the righteous is a man of injustice, and an abomination to a wicked person is one of upright way.
verses.30:1: The words of Agur son of Jakeh, the oracle. The utterance of the man to Ithiel, to Ithiel and Ucal:
verses.30:2: Surely I am more brutish than any man, and I have no human understanding.
verses.30:3: And I have not learned wisdom, nor do I know the knowledge of the Holy One.
verses.30:4: Who has ascended to the heavens and descended? Who has gathered the wind in his cupped hands? Who has bound up the waters in a cloak? Who has set in place all the ends of the earth? What is his name, and what is his son's name, if you know?
verses.30:5: Every utterance of God is refined; He is a shield for those who seek refuge in Him.
verses.30:6: Do not add to His words, or else He will rebuke you and you will be proven false.
verses.30:7: Two things I have asked from You; do not withhold them from me before I die:
verses.30:8: Put deceit and a lying word far from me; do not give me poverty or wealth; feed me the bread of my allotted portion,
verses.30:9: or else I might be satisfied and disown You and say, "Who is the LORD?" or else I might become impoverished and steal and violate the name of my God.
verses.30:10: Do not malign a servant to his master, or else he will curse you and you will incur guilt.
verses.30:11: There is a generation that curses its father and does not bless its mother.
verses.30:12: There is a generation that is pure in its own eyes, yet has not been washed from its filth.
verses.30:13: There is a generation—how lofty are its eyes, and its eyelids are lifted up!
verses.30:14: There is a generation whose teeth are swords and whose jaw-teeth are knives, to devour the afflicted from the earth and the needy from among humanity.
verses.30:15: The leech has two daughters: "Give! Give!" There are three things that are never satisfied, four that do not say, "Enough":
verses.30:16: Sheol, and a closed womb, earth that is not satisfied with water, and fire that does not say, "Enough."
verses.30:17: An eye that mocks a father and despises obedience to a mother—ravens of the valley will gouge it out, and young eagles will eat it.
verses.30:18: There are three things too marvelous for me, and four that I do not know:
verses.30:19: the way of the eagle in the heavens, the way of a serpent over a rock, the way of a ship in the heart of the sea, and the way of a man with a young woman.
verses.30:20: Such is the way of an adulterous woman: she eats and wipes her mouth, and says, "I have done no iniquity."
verses.30:21: Beneath three things the earth trembles, and beneath four it cannot endure:
verses.30:22: beneath a servant when he becomes king, and a fool when he is satisfied with bread;
verses.30:23: beneath a hated woman when she is married, and a maidservant when she dispossesses her mistress.
verses.30:24: Four are the small things of the earth, yet they are supremely wise:
verses.30:25: the ants are a people without strength, yet they prepare their food in summer;
verses.30:26: rock hyraxes are a people without might, yet they set their house in the cliff;
verses.30:27: locusts have no king, yet they all march out in divisions;
verses.30:28: a lizard you can catch with the hands, yet it is in a king's palaces.
verses.30:29: There are three things splendid in stride, and four that are splendid in walking:
verses.30:30: a lion, mighty among the beasts, and it does not turn back before anything;
verses.30:31: a strutting rooster, or a male goat, and a king against whom there is no rising up.
verses.30:32: If you have acted foolishly in lifting yourself up, or if you have schemed, put your hand to your mouth.
verses.30:33: For squeezing milk brings out curds, and squeezing the nose brings out blood, and squeezing anger brings out strife.
verses.31:1: The words of King Lemuel, an oracle with which his mother instructed him.
verses.31:2: What, my son? And what, son of my womb? And what, son of my vows?
verses.31:3: Do not give women your vigor, nor your ways to what ruins kings.
verses.31:4: Not for kings, Lemuel; not for kings is drinking wine, nor for rulers to ask, "Where is strong drink?"
verses.31:5: Otherwise they may drink and forget what has been decreed, and subvert the cause of all who are afflicted.
verses.31:6: Give strong drink to someone who is perishing, and wine to those bitter of soul.
verses.31:7: May he drink and forget his poverty, and no longer remember his hardship.
verses.31:8: Open your mouth on behalf of the mute, for the cause of all who face ruin.
verses.31:9: Open your mouth, judge with righteousness, and defend the cause of the afflicted and the needy.
verses.31:10: Who can find a woman of valor? For far beyond jewels is her worth.
verses.31:11: Her husband's heart trusts in her, and he will not lack gain.
verses.31:12: She bestows good on him, and not harm, all the days of her life.
verses.31:13: She seeks out wool and flax, and works gladly with her hands.
verses.31:14: She is like a merchant's ships; from a distance she brings her food.
verses.31:15: She rises while night still remains, and gives provisions to her household and an allotted portion to her servant women.
verses.31:16: She evaluates a field and acquires it; from the fruit of her hands she plants a vineyard.
verses.31:17: She binds her waist with strength and fortifies her arms.
verses.31:18: She discerns that her merchandise is good; at night her lamp does not go out.
verses.31:19: She extends her hands to the distaff, and her palms grip the spindle.
verses.31:20: She spreads open her palm to the afflicted, and extends both her hands to the needy.
verses.31:21: She does not fear snow for her household, because her entire household is clothed in scarlet.
verses.31:22: She makes tapestries for herself; fine linen and purple are her clothing.
verses.31:23: Her husband is known at the gates as he sits with the elders of the land.
verses.31:24: She makes linen wraps and sells them, and supplies belts to the trader.
verses.31:26: Strength and splendor are her clothing, and she laughs at the day to come.
verses.31:27: She keeps watch over the ways of her household, and the bread of idleness she does not eat.
verses.31:28: With wisdom she opens her mouth, and instruction of kindness is on her tongue. Her children rise and pronounce her blessed; her husband as well, and he praises her:
verses.31:29: "Many daughters have acted valiantly, but you have risen above them all."
verses.31:30: Charm is deception and beauty is a vapor; a woman who fears the LORD, she is the one to be praised.
verses.31:31: Give her from the fruit of her hands, and let her deeds praise her at the gates.

notes.1:17: Literally "every owner of a wing" (kol-ba'al kanaf), an idiom for any winged creature; Hebrew chinnam ("in vain") echoes the same word in 1:11 ("without cause"), underscoring the irony that the wicked walk into their own trap.
notes.1:20: Hebrew chokhmot is a feminine plural form used as an abstract intensive for personified Wisdom, governed by singular verbs in 1:20b-21 (titten, tiqra, tomer; taronnah is formally feminine plural or an uncommon 3fs form).
notes.1:27: Qere reads kesho'ah ("like a tempest"); ketiv ksh'wh is an orthographic variant of the same word.
notes.1:31: Hebrew mo'atsotehem ("their own counsels") shares the same root (y-'-ts) as Wisdom's atsati ("my counsel") in 1:25 and 1:30.
notes.2:7: Qere reads yitspon (Qal imperfect 3ms, "He stores up"); ketiv reads wtspn ("and He stored up" or "and a store").
notes.2:16: Literally "a strange woman" (ishshah zarah) and "a foreign woman" (nokhriyyah), idioms denoting a woman outside the marriage bond, i.e., an adulterous woman (cf. 2:17).
notes.2:18: Hebrew shachah (Qal perfect 3fs of shuach, "sinks down") is feminine despite bayit ("house") normally being masculine; repha'im ("departed spirits") denotes the shades of the dead in the underworld.
notes.2:22: Hebrew yissechu is Qal imperfect 3mp of nasach ("they will tear out"), used impersonally with passive force ("will be torn out").
notes.3:8: Hebrew lesharekha follows the Masoretic vocalization of shor ("navel"), denoting the core of the body; the Septuagint reflects a different reading ("your flesh/body").
notes.3:12: Hebrew ukhe'av ("just as a father") follows the Masoretic vocalization, with the Hiphil verb yokhiach ("reproves") carried over from the first clause; the Septuagint reads the consonants as a verb ("causes pain / scourges").
notes.3:27: Follows the Qere yadekha (singular, "your hand") in the idiom "in the power of your hand," whereas the Ketiv reads plural yadeikha ("your hands"). Hebrew mibbe'alav literally means "from its owners."
notes.3:34: Follows the Qere vela'anavim ("and to the humble"), whereas the Ketiv reads vela'aniyyim ("and to the afflicted/poor"). In the first clause, the Hiphil verb yalits ("scoffs") echoes the cognate participle letsim ("scoffers").
notes.3:35: Hebrew merim is a singular Hiphil participle of rum ("lifts up / carries off") used distributively with plural kesilim ("fools"), similar to 3:18; alternatively, qalon ("disgrace") may be taken as subject ("disgrace exalts fools").
notes.4:13: The feminine object suffix on nitsreha ("guard her") and feminine pronoun hi' ("she") refer either back to feminine wisdom (4:5-11) or to discipline (musar, normally masculine) personified alongside wisdom.
notes.4:16: Follows the Qere yakhshilu (Hiphil imperfect of kashal, "they cause someone to stumble"), whereas the Ketiv reads yikhsholu (Qal imperfect, "they stumble").
notes.4:18: Hebrew holekh va'or (literally "going and brightening") is an idiom for continuous increase, and nekhon hayyom (Niphal participle of kun in construct with "the day") literally denotes "the established point of the day," meaning full daylight or midday.
notes.4:23: Hebrew mikkol-mishmar uses the comparative preposition min ("above / more than all that is kept"), and totse'ot chayyim literally means "the outgoings" or "sources of life."
notes.4:26: Hebrew palles (Piel imperative of palas) can mean either "weigh / examine carefully" or "make level" (compare Isaiah 26:7); both lead to the result that all one's ways "will be firm" (yikkonu, Niphal imperfect of kun).
notes.5:3: Hebrew zarah ("a strange woman") denotes a woman outside one's own marriage and household, that is, an adulteress, paired with nokriyyah ("a foreign woman") in v. 20. Literally "her palate" (hikkah) is used by metonymy for seductive speech.
notes.5:6: Both verbs (Piel imperfect tefalles, "weigh/level," and Qal imperfect teda, "know") can be parsed as either 3rd feminine singular ("she") or 2nd masculine singular ("you"). Reading them as 3rd feminine singular treats pen as an emphatic negation continuing the description of the strange woman from vv. 3-5; read as 2nd masculine singular, the clause warns, "so that you do not weigh the path of life, her tracks wander without your knowing."
notes.5:16: The Masoretic Text has no interrogative particle here, but the contrast with v. 17 ("to you alone, and none to strangers") supports reading the verse as an unmarked rhetorical question; alternatively it may be read as a jussive wish, "May your springs disperse outside."
notes.5:19: The Qal verb shagah ("reel, stagger, go astray") creates a deliberate wordplay across vv. 19, 20, and 23, moving from joyful intoxication with one's own wife (v. 19) to illicit infatuation with a strange woman (v. 20) and fatal wandering through folly (v. 23).
notes.6:5: The Masoretic Text literally reads miyyad ("from the hand") without specifying "of the hunter," leaving the parallel term yaqush ("a trapper") in the second clause to supply the implied agent.
notes.6:14: Ketiv reads medanim (as in v. 19) while Qere reads midyanim; both are plural nouns meaning "quarrels/strife," and the translation follows the Qere.
notes.6:16: Ketiv reads the plural to'evot ("abominations"), whereas Qere reads the singular construct to'avat ("an abomination"); the translation follows the singular Qere.
notes.6:22: The verbs tanheh (Hiphil imperfect), tishmor (Qal imperfect), and teshiheka (Qal imperfect), together with the explicit pronoun hi, shift from the plural "them" in v. 21 to feminine singular ("it"), referring to the mother's torah ("teaching") or to parental instruction as a single whole.
notes.6:26: The opening clause is elliptical (literally "for a prostitute woman, up to a loaf of bread"), contrasting the small fee of a prostitute with the fatal cost of adultery with a married woman. An older grammatical reading supplies a passive verb: "on account of a prostitute, one is reduced to a loaf of bread."
notes.7:5: The phrases "strange woman" (ishah zarah) and "foreign woman" (nokriyyah) are recurring Proverbs idioms for an illicit or outside woman, that is, an adulteress. The verb hecheliqah is Hiphil of chalaq ("make smooth"), denoting flattering or seductive speech.
notes.7:9: The noun ishon, which means "pupil" of the eye in 7:2, is used metaphorically here for the darkest center or "dead" of night, verbally linking the young man's folly back to the father's warning.
notes.7:10: The construct phrase netsurat lev (Qal passive participle of natsar, "guard/keep hidden," plus lev, "heart") literally means "guarded/hidden of heart," describing a woman who conceals her scheming intent.
notes.7:16: Both chatuvot ("colored/striped cloths") and the Egyptian loanword etun ("fine linen/yarn," a hapax legomenon) are rare textile terms; the verb ravadti ("I have spread") is cognate with marvaddim ("tapestries").
notes.7:22: The Masoretic clause ukhe'ekes el-musar evil literally reads "and like a fetter to the discipline of a fool," a compressed expression rendered here without adopting ancient versional emendations.
notes.8:17: Ketiv reads "those who love her" (third-person feminine singular suffix), whereas the qere followed here reads "those who love me" (first-person singular suffix), matching Wisdom's first-person address.
notes.8:22: The Qal verb qanah ("acquired") primarily means "acquire" or "possess" throughout Proverbs, though in poetic creation contexts (compare Gen 14:19; Deut 32:6) it can also carry the sense "bring forth" or "create."
notes.8:23: The Niphal perfect nissakti comes from nasak ("install/appoint," as in Ps 2:6, or "pour out/cast"), though some lexicons connect the form to sakak ("weave/form," compare Ps 139:13).
notes.8:30: The noun amon is a famous lexical crux, understood either as "master artisan/craftsman" (compare Akkadian ummanu) or, connecting it with aman ("nurse/raise"), as "ward" or "nursling."
notes.8:35: Ketiv writes the verb with a final yod (either dittography from the preceding "the one who finds me" or a plural participle "finders of"), while the qere followed here is the Qal perfect third-person masculine singular matsa ("has found"), matching the singular verb "gains" in the second clause.
notes.9:1: Hebrew hokmot is plural in form construed with a singular verb, an abstract plural of fullness personifying Wisdom.
notes.9:6: Hebrew petayim is the plural of peti ("naive"), functioning here either as an abstract plural ("naivety") or concretely ("leave the company of the naive").
notes.9:10: Hebrew qedoshim ("holy ones") is plural in form, functioning here as a plural of majesty for "the Holy One" in parallel with "the LORD."
notes.9:18: Hebrew rephaim refers to the departed spirits or shades of the dead dwelling in Sheol; "her invited guests" literally renders the passive participle of qara ("those she called"), echoing her call in 9:15.
notes.10:4: Hebrew rash ("impoverished") and oseh ("working") are both masculine singular participles, indicating a person working with a slack hand rather than taking the feminine noun kaph ("hand") as subject.
notes.10:6: Because both "the mouth of the wicked" and "violence" are masculine singular without an object marker, the Hebrew clause (repeated verbatim in 10:11) can be read either as "the mouth of the wicked hides violence" or "violence covers the mouth of the wicked."
notes.10:8: The rare Niphal verb yillabet (found only here, 10:10, and Hosea 4:14) denotes being thrust down or falling to ruin; in 10:10 the Masoretic Hebrew repeats this entire second line verbatim.
notes.10:17: Hebrew literally equates the one who keeps discipline with "a path to life" (though some read an implied "on the path to life"); matteh is a Hiphil participle meaning "causes to stray," though sometimes taken intransitively as "goes astray."
notes.10:22: The verb "brings wealth" is feminine singular, agreeing with "blessing," while "does not add" shifts to masculine singular with "the LORD" as subject and the feminine suffix "with it" referring back to the blessing; alternatively, the second clause can be read "and toil adds nothing to it."
notes.11:3: The Qere (read text) has the Qal imperfect yeshoddem ('ruins them,' from shadad), matching the imperfect verb in the first clause; the Ketiv (written text) has an initial waw instead of yod, likely an orthographic variant.
notes.11:7: Hebrew onim is the plural of on ('strength' or 'wealth'); some interpreters instead relate it to awen ('iniquity').
notes.11:15: Hebrew ra-yeroa pairs a cognate noun with a Niphal verb from the root meaning 'to shatter/come to harm' for emphasis; 'hand-pledges' renders toqim, literally 'those who strike [hands],' referring to sealing a surety agreement.
notes.11:21: 'Rest assured' translates the Hebrew idiom yad leyad, literally 'hand to hand,' expressing a solemn pledge or certainty.
notes.11:25: The rare verb form yore is taken as a passive (Hophal) or by-form meaning 'will be watered/refreshed,' answering the Hiphil participle marweh ('one who waters') in the same clause.
notes.12:12: Hebrew metsod can mean 'hunting net' or 'catch/spoil,' and the Qal imperfect yitten literally means 'gives,' used absolutely here for producing fruit.
notes.12:14: The Qere (read text) has the Hiphil imperfect yashiv ('will be repaid,' literally 'one will render back'), whereas the Ketiv (written text) has the Qal yashuv ('will return').
notes.12:26: Hebrew yater mereehu is ambiguous: it is translated here as the Hiphil of tur ('guides') with the noun merea ('companion'), though it can also be parsed as 'excels/is superior to his neighbor' or 'examines his friend.'
notes.12:27: The rare verb yacharok ('roast') occurs only here in the Hebrew Bible and is clarified by Aramaic and later Hebrew cognates; the compressed second clause literally reads 'and a person's wealth, precious, diligence' (or 'precious is a diligent person's wealth').
notes.12:28: The Masoretic text reads al-mawet ('no death'), a rare use of the negative particle al directly before a noun rather than the preposition el ('to'), following the phrase derek netivah ('way of a pathway').
notes.13:6: Both objects use abstract nouns for concrete persons: the first literally means 'blamelessness of way' (standing for the blameless person), and the second literally means 'sin' (standing for the sinner).
notes.13:8: The Hebrew noun rendered 'rebuke' (the same word used in v. 1) can also carry the contextual sense 'threat,' contrasting the rich person who must ransom his life with the poor person who faces no extortion threat.
notes.13:11: 'From emptiness' translates Hebrew mehebel (lit. 'from vapor/emptiness,' i.e., fleeting or futile schemes), and 'handful by handful' renders the idiom al-yad (lit. 'upon hand,' meaning gradually or by steady labor).
notes.13:15: The Masoretic text reads etan ('perennial, unyielding, rough'), depicting the way of the treacherous as hard and rugged terrain.
notes.13:20: Ketiv/Qere: the Qere reads a participle and imperfect ('One who walks... will grow wise'), whereas the Ketiv reads an infinitive absolute and imperative ('Walk with the wise and become wise').
notes.14:9: Because the Hiphil verb 'mocks' is singular while 'fools' is plural, singular 'guilt' (which can also mean 'guilt offering') is taken here as the subject; alternatively, taking 'fools' distributively, 'Fools mock at guilt (or the guilt offering).'
notes.14:14: Hebrew literally reads 'and from upon him' (i.e., from himself or from his own ways), with the verb 'will be filled' implied from the first clause.
notes.14:21: Ketiv/Qere: the Qere reads 'the humble' (or 'the afflicted'), whereas the Ketiv reads 'the poor' (or 'the needy').
notes.14:32: The Masoretic text reads 'in his death,' affirming the righteous person's enduring trust even in death; 'by his evil' in the first clause can also mean 'in his calamity.'
notes.14:34: Hebrew chesed here is a rare homonym meaning 'disgrace' or 'reproach' (cf. Lev 20:17), distinct from chesed ('loyal love') in v. 22.
notes.15:11: Abaddon (Hebrew avaddon, 'destruction') is a poetic synonym for Sheol, the realm of the dead.
notes.15:14: Translated from the Qere ufi ('and the mouth of'); the Ketiv reads ufenei ('and the face of').
notes.15:22: The Hiphil infinitive absolute hafer ('frustrating') functions impersonally ('plans are thwarted'), and the feminine singular verb taqum ('it stands') refers collectively to 'plans' (mahashavot).
notes.15:27: The second sentence is Masoretic 16:6, carried in this verse following the Saints (Greek) verse order.
notes.15:28: The second sentence is Masoretic 16:7, carried in this verse following the Saints (Greek) verse order.
notes.15:29: The second and third sentences are Masoretic 16:8 and 16:9, carried in this verse following the Saints (Greek) verse order.
notes.15:30: The Piel verb tedashen literally means 'makes fat' (fills with marrow and vitality), an idiom for nourishing or restoring health.
notes.16:5: Hebrew yad leyad ('hand to hand') is an oath or handshake idiom expressing firm assurance, and the Niphal yinnaqeh means 'be cleared of guilt' or 'go unpunished.'
notes.16:9: The third-person suffix on lamma'anehu can refer either to each created thing ('for its purpose') or to the LORD ('for His own purpose').
notes.16:19: Translated from the Qere anavim ('the humble'); the Ketiv reads aniyyim ('the poor' or 'the afflicted').
notes.16:26: Hebrew nefesh here denotes physical appetite or hunger, and the hapax verb akhaf ('presses upon') conveys the relentless urgency of needing food.
notes.16:27: Translated from the Qere sefato (singular, 'his lip'); the Ketiv reads sefatav (dual, 'his lips').
notes.17:11: Hebrew fronts the object 'only rebellion' before the verb 'seeks' and subject 'an evil person' (some alternatively read 'a rebellious person seeks only evil').
notes.17:13: Ketiv/qere variant: the qere reads the Qal imperfect 'tamush' ('will depart'), whereas the ketiv writes the Hiphil 'tamish', used intransitively with essentially the same sense.
notes.17:22: Hebrew 'yeitiv gehah' pairs the Hiphil imperfect of 'yatav' ('make good/improve') with the hapax legomenon 'gehah' ('healing/cure', cognate with the verb 'yigheh' in Hos 5:13).
notes.17:27: Ketiv/qere variant: this translates the qere 'yeqar-ruach' ('restrained/sparing of spirit', from 'yaqar' meaning rare/prized, cf. Prov 25:17), while the ketiv writes 'veqar-ruach' ('and cool of spirit').
notes.18:1: The verb 'yitgalla' ('erupts/breaks out') is the rare Hithpael of 'gala', appearing elsewhere in the Hebrew Bible only in Prov 17:14 and 20:3.
notes.18:8: Hebrew 'mitlahamim' is a rare Hithpael participle occurring only here and in Prov 26:22; based on Semitic cognates meaning to swallow greedily, it denotes choice or tasty morsels, though older versions sometimes rendered it 'wounds'.
notes.18:17: Ketiv/qere variant: the qere reads 'uva' (conjunction 'vav' plus Qal perfect, 'but ... comes'), whereas the ketiv writes the imperfect 'yavo' without the conjunction.
notes.18:19: Ketiv/qere variant: the qere reads 'umidyanim' ('and contentions', matching v. 18), while the ketiv writes the synonymous plural 'umedonim'. The first clause uses an elliptical comparative 'min' ('than') with 'nifsha', the sole Niphal occurrence of 'pasha' ('transgress/wrong').
notes.19:7: Ketiv reads "lo'" ("not"), yielding "he pursues words, but they are gone"; the translated qere reads "lo" ("to him" / "his"), yielding "they belong to him" (meaning his words remain only with himself).
notes.19:16: Ketiv reads the Hophal "yumat" ("will be put to death"); the translated qere reads the Qal "yamut" ("will die").
notes.19:19: Ketiv reads "grl" (possibly "harsh of" or a graphic resh/dalet variant); the translated qere reads "gedol-chemah" ("great of wrath," i.e., a person of great wrath).
notes.19:27: The Qal imperative "stop/cease" followed by the infinitive construct "to wander/stray" functions conditionally or ironically to state the consequence of ignoring discipline; alternatively, the clause warns against instruction that causes straying.
notes.20:4: Ketiv reads the asyndetic Qal imperfect "yish'al" ("he begs/seeks"); the translated qere reads the waw-consecutive Qal perfect "wesha'al" ("so he begs/seeks").
notes.20:9: The sentences after the first are Masoretic 20:20-22, carried in this verse following the Saints (Greek) verse order. Translated qere readings: be'eshun ("in deep darkness"; ketiv be'ishon, "in the pupil/middle of darkness") and the Pual participle mevohelet ("gained hastily"; ketiv mevuchelet, "gained greedily" or "loathed").
notes.20:25: The rare verb "yala'" denotes speaking rashly or blurting out a dedicatory declaration ("It is sacred"); an older interpretation connected it to a root meaning "to swallow/devour" something holy.
notes.20:30: Ketiv reads "tamriq" (a Hiphil verbal form "scours away" or a variant noun); the translated qere reads the noun "tamruq" ("a scouring / cleansing").
notes.21:4: Hebrew nir (defective spelling of nir) can mean either lamp (a variant of ner, as in 1 Kgs 11:36 and 2 Sam 22:29, matching Prov 13:9 and 24:20) or freshly plowed ground (as in Prov 13:23). Both senses fit the Masoretic vocalization, though lamp accords closely with the surrounding imagery in Proverbs.
notes.21:6: The Masoretic Text reads mevaqshei-mavet (Piel participle of baqash, 'those who seek death'), standing in terse apposition to the preceding phrase. Some ancient versions instead reflect moqshei-mavet ('snares of death').
notes.21:8: Hebrew vazar is a hapax legomenon meaning guilty or laden with guilt (cognate with Arabic wizr), forming a direct antonym to zakh ('pure') in the second clause. Some earlier interpreters divided it as ve-zar ('and strange').
notes.21:12: Hebrew tsaddiq ('Righteous One') lacks an article, as poetic epithets for God often do, and is widely understood as referring to God because the same subject overturns the wicked to ruin (compare 22:12). Others understand it as a righteous human observer.
notes.21:29: The translation follows the Masoretic Qere yavin darko ('considers his way', from bin with a singular noun). The Ketiv reads yakhin derakhav ('establishes his ways', Hiphil of kun with a plural noun).
notes.22:11: The translation follows the Masoretic Qere tohar-lev ('purity of heart', construct noun). The Ketiv reads tahor ('pure', adjective).
notes.22:16: The Hebrew is terse and asyndetic, juxtaposing two participles ('one who oppresses... one who gives...') before the single predicate 'only to want.' Both exploiting the poor for personal gain and currying favor with the rich end in poverty.
notes.22:20: The translation follows the vocalized Masoretic Qere shalishim ('noble things', plural of shalish, officer or noble, comparable to Prov 8:6). The Ketiv reads shilshom ('formerly' or 'previously'), while many scholars revocalize the Qere as sheloshim ('thirty' sayings).
notes.22:21: Hebrew qosht ('reliability' or 'truth') is a rare noun cognate with Aramaic qeshot ('truth'). The final participle sholekhekha ('those who sent you') is masculine plural in the Masoretic Text.
notes.22:23: The rare verb qava ('despoil' or 'rob', elsewhere only in Mal 3:8-9) is repeated in a double-accusative construction ('despoil those who despoil them of life') to highlight poetic retribution.
notes.23:5: Two ketiv/qere variants occur here: the read qere has Hiphil 'will you cause your eyes to fly' (ketiv Qal) and Qal 'it flies' (ketiv a defective form), creating wordplay on the Hebrew root for flying.
notes.23:7: The rare verb rendered 'reckons' occurs only here in the Hebrew Bible and denotes inward calculation or tallying, fitting the stingy host of verses 6-8.
notes.23:24: Three ketiv/qere variants occur here: the read qere uses the infinitive absolute of the root for exulting (ketiv an alternate hollow spelling) and places the conjunction 'and' before 'the one who fathers' rather than before 'will be glad in him.'
notes.23:26: The read qere has 'watch' (from the root for guarding or observing), whereas the written ketiv has 'delight in' (from a different root meaning to take pleasure in).
notes.23:29: The read qere and written ketiv are variant plural forms of the same noun meaning 'quarrels' or 'contentions.'
notes.23:31: The read qere has 'in the cup,' whereas the written ketiv reads 'in the purse' or 'bag'; 'gives its gleam' is literally 'gives its eye,' a Hebrew idiom for surface sparkle.
notes.24:10: The Hebrew plays on two words from the same root: 'distress' (tsarah) and 'meager' (tsar, literally 'narrow').
notes.24:11: The Hebrew particle 'im' with the imperfect ('surely hold back') functions here as an emphatic entreaty, though some read it conditionally as an ellipsis ('if you hold back').
notes.24:17: The read qere is singular 'your enemy,' matching the singular suffix in 'when he stumbles,' whereas the written ketiv is plural 'your enemies.'
notes.24:21: The Qal participle rendered 'those prone to change' literally means 'those who change' or 'differ,' referring here to fickle people or political dissenters.
notes.24:28: Following the Masoretic vocalization, the second verb combines the conjunction 'and,' the interrogative prefix, and a Piel perfect ('and would you deceive?') as a rhetorical question.
notes.24:34: Unlike the parallel in 6:11, the Masoretic Text here uses the Hithpael participle 'prowling' without a comparative preposition, along with plural 'your needs'; 'an armed warrior' is literally 'a man of a shield.'
notes.25:7: The Masoretic verse division keeps the final clause, "whom your eyes have seen," at the end of 25:7 modifying "a noble," whereas some ancient versions attach it to the opening of 25:8.
notes.25:11: The noun translated "silver settings" denotes figured or carved ornamental work, and the final word translated "at its proper moment" is a Hebrew hapax legomenon whose exact sense is debated, often associated with fitting turns or circumstances.
notes.25:24: The Qere reads midyanim and the Ketiv reads medonim, a minor morphological variant with the same sense ("quarrels" or "contentions"); the same Ketiv/Qere pair recurs in 26:21.
notes.25:27: The second clause is notoriously terse in the Masoretic Text, literally "and searching out their glory [is] glory"; the negative from "not good" in the first half is widely taken to carry over into the second clause, with the third-person plural suffix used indefinitely ("one's own").
notes.26:2: Translates the Qere lo ("to him"), traditionally understood to mean that an undeserved curse returns upon the one who utters it; the Ketiv reads lo' ("not"), meaning a causeless curse does not arrive or alight.
notes.26:7: The opening verb dalyu is a rare and anomalous form generally derived from a root meaning to hang limp or dangle uselessly.
notes.26:8: The noun margemah ("sling") occurs only here in the Hebrew Bible; while most lexicons understand the phrase as binding a stone into a sling, some interpret it as placing a pebble on a stone heap.
notes.26:10: One of the most lexically difficult verses in Proverbs; rendering the opening words as "an archer piercing everyone" preserves the Masoretic consonants and matches the surrounding proverbs about fools, though the same words can also be construed as "a master who produces everything."
notes.26:22: The Hithpael participle translated "savory morsels" occurs only here and in Proverbs 18:8; it is generally explained from a cognate root meaning to swallow greedily, though older interpretations sometimes rendered it as "wounds."
notes.27:6: The Niphal participle natarot from atar means profuse or excessive, contrasting with the trustworthy wounds of one who loves, though some understand it by contrast as deceitful.
notes.27:9: The Hebrew me'atsat-nefesh is literally from counsel of the soul, denoting heartfelt or sincere counsel; some alternatively take the preposition comparatively as sweeter than one's own counsel.
notes.27:15: The verb nishtawah is a rare Nithpael hybrid passive-reflexive form of shawah meaning be alike or matched. The ketiv reads medonim and the qere reads midyanim, a variant noun pattern of the same word for quarrels or contentions.
notes.27:16: The final clause is difficult; yiqra is taken here from qara II meaning meet or encounter, picturing a hand trying to grasp slippery oil, though some take it from qara I meaning oil announces itself on his right hand.
notes.27:24: The ketiv reads dor without the conjunction, while the qere reads wador, yielding the standard idiom from generation to generation.
notes.28:2: Following the Masoretic disjunctive accent on yodea, ken is taken as right order or stability with the intransitive Hiphil ya'arikh meaning lasts long; alternatively, ken may be adverbial meaning so or thus it endures.
notes.28:12: The Pual imperfect yechuppas from chapas literally means is searched for, implying that people go into hiding when the wicked rise, paralleling yissater in 28:28.
notes.28:16: The ketiv reads the plural construct form sone'e meaning haters of, while the qere reads the singular participle sone meaning one who hates, agreeing with the singular Hiphil verb ya'arikh.
notes.28:18: Hebrew derakhayim is a dual form meaning two ways, conveying duplicity as in 28:6, creating a wordplay with the feminine singular be'achat, which can mean either in one of them or idiomatically at once.
notes.28:23: Hebrew acharay is pointed like after me, but is widely understood as an unusual adverbial form of achar meaning afterward or in the end.
notes.29:4: Hebrew ish terumot literally means 'a man of contributions,' using terumah (ordinarily a sacred offering) here for royal exactions or bribes.
notes.29:10: Hebrew literally reads 'but the upright seek his life,' using the Piel of baqash ('seek') here in a protective sense of caring for the blameless person's life rather than its usual hostile idiom elsewhere.
notes.29:11: Hebrew be'achor yeshabbechennah literally means 'stills it in the rear,' using the Piel of shabach ('calm, still') for holding one's spirit quietly in reserve.
notes.29:21: Hebrew manon is a hapax legomenon of uncertain meaning, often derived from the root nun ('offspring') to mean 'heir' or 'son,' though others understand it as 'grief' or 'ingrate.'
notes.30:1: The Masoretic Text points hammassa as 'the oracle' (though some read it as a place or tribal name, 'of Massa') and vocalizes le'iti'el and ve'ukal as personal names ('to Ithiel, to Ithiel and Ucal'), which many scholars repoint as a cry of weariness ('I am weary, God... and spent').
notes.30:3: Hebrew qedoshim is a plural of majesty for 'the Holy One' (as in 9:10), and the negative particle lo ('not') in the first clause carries over into the second clause.
notes.30:18: Ketiv reads the feminine numeral ve'arba ('and four'); Qere reads the masculine ve'arba'ah to agree with masculine sheloshah ('three') and the masculine suffix on yeda'tim ('I know them').
notes.30:28: The Piel imperfect tetappes is ambiguous in person and gender: it may be parsed as second-person masculine singular ('you can catch with the hands') or as third-person feminine singular with 'lizard' as subject ('it grasps with its hands').
notes.30:31: Hebrew zarzir motnayim literally means 'girded of loins,' an uncertain creature traditionally identified as a strutting rooster or a greyhound; alqum immo literally reads 'no rising up against him' (al plus qum), though some compare Arabic al-qawm ('with his army with him').
notes.31:3: The form lamchot is commonly analyzed as a Hiphil infinitive construct of mchh with elided he ("to destroying/ruining"), governing the Aramaic-style plural melakin ("kings").
notes.31:4: Ketiv/Qere: Qere reads ei ("where?"), rendered here as rulers asking "Where is strong drink?"; Ketiv has the consonants aleph-waw, often vocalized as a noun meaning "desire" (from the root avah) or taken as "or".
notes.31:16: Ketiv/Qere: Qere reads the third-person feminine singular Qal perfect nate'ah ("she plants"), agreeing with the feminine subject; Ketiv omits the final he.
notes.31:27: Ketiv/Qere: Qere reads halikhot ("ways" or "activities"), plural of halikhah; Ketiv transposes the yod and lamed and omits the plural waw.
notes.31:28: The Hebrew numbers the Ayin line ('Strength and splendor are her clothing') as 31:25 and the Pe line ('With wisdom she opens her mouth') as 31:26; this edition shows the Ayin line at 31:26 and joins the Pe line to the Qoph line here at 31:28, with no separate 31:25.

unplaced.text: The beginning of wisdom: acquire wisdom, and with all your possessions, acquire understanding.
unplaced.note: Or 'at the cost of all you possess.'

unplaced.text: Listen to discipline and become wise, and do not disregard it.
Wealth brings no benefit on the day of wrath, but righteousness rescues from death.
An ear that listens to life-giving correction will lodge among the wise.
The preparations of the heart belong to a person, but the response of the tongue comes from the LORD.
Entrust your works to the LORD, and your plans will stand firm.
unplaced.note: Literally 'Roll your works onto the LORD.'

unplaced.text: A poor man speaks with pleas for mercy, but a rich man replies with harsh words.
A man with many companions is bound for ruin, yet there is a friend who clings closer than a brother.
unplaced.note: Hebrew plays on the similar sounds of 'companions' and 'ruin'; some interpret the verb as 'to act as a companion.'

unplaced.text: A poor man who walks in his integrity is better than one whose lips are crooked and who is a fool.
Moreover, a soul without knowledge is not good, and one who rushes with his feet misses the mark.
unplaced.note: Here 'soul' can also mean 'desire,' and 'misses the mark' can also mean 'sins.'

unplaced.text: "No good, no good," the buyer says, but once he walks off, then he boasts.
There is gold and an abundance of rubies, yet lips of knowledge are a precious ornament.
Take his garment, since he has put up security for a stranger, and hold him in pledge on behalf of a foreign woman.
unplaced.note: Following the traditional reading 'a foreign woman'; the written consonantal text reads 'foreigners.'

unplaced.text: Sweet to a man is bread of deceit, but afterward his mouth will fill with gravel.
Plans stand firm through counsel; wage war with skillful guidance.
One who goes about as a gossip exposes a secret; do not associate with anyone who opens his lips wide.
The plans of a diligent person certainly bring abundance, but everyone who rushes certainly comes to poverty.
Train a child according to his way; even when he grows old, he will not turn aside from it.
unplaced.note: Literally 'according to the mouth of his way,' meaning either the path suited to him or the way he ought to go.

unplaced.text: Acquire truth and do not sell it—wisdom, discipline, and understanding.
